question: How does the text describe Hannah's situation at home and during the yearly trips to Shiloh?
Why does Eli misread Hannah's prayer, and what changes in his attitude after she explains herself?
The verb שָׁאַל (sha'al, “ask”) returns at the end of the chapter: how does it link Hannah's request to the name of Samuel and to what she does with the boy?
Hannah says she has been “pouring out” her soul before the LORD: what do you usually do with the anguish you cannot say out loud?
In Hannah's song, what reversals of fortune appear between the strong and the weak, the full and the hungry, the rich and the poor?
The verb רוּם (rum, “exalt, lift up”) opens and closes the song: who is exalted at the beginning, who at the end, and what does this frame suggest?
The narrator alternates the sins of Eli's sons with news of the boy Samuel: what effect does this contrast have on the reading?
The man of God accuses Eli of honoring his sons more than God: how does this show in the acts described in the chapter?
“Those who honor Me I will honor”: in what concrete choices of your routine could this sentence carry weight?
How many times is Samuel called, to whom does he run, and what does Eli finally understand?
The verb קָרָא (qara', “call”) is repeated throughout the scene: what does the insistence of this call say about the way God approaches Samuel?
Why does the text note at the start that “the word of the LORD was rare in those days,” and how does the end of the chapter answer this?
“Speak, for Your servant is listening”: what would help you listen better, whether to God or to the people around you?
What do the elders of Israel decide after the first defeat, and what happens in the second battle?
How do the Israelites and the Philistines seem to understand the presence of the ark in the camp, and what does the outcome say about this idea?
The verb לָקַח (laqach, “take, capture”) appears in the phrase “the ark of God has been captured,” repeated to the end: why does this news weigh more than the deaths?
Phinehas's wife sums it all up in “Ichabod”: what loss has made you feel that the “glory” had departed?
What happens to the statue of Dagon on two mornings in a row, and in what position is it found?
The expression “the hand of the LORD,” with יָד (yad, “hand”), is repeated in Ashdod, Gath and Ekron: what does this image communicate about who acts in history?
Why does the ark pass from city to city, and what does this “journey” reveal about the Philistines?
The people of Ashdod want the ark far away because it bothers them: is there something in your life you prefer to push away instead of facing it?
How do the Philistines set up the test with the cows and the cart, and what do the cows do on the way?
The noun אָשָׁם (asham, “guilt offering”) appears on the Philistines' lips: what do they acknowledge by returning the ark with this kind of offering?
Why do the people of Beth-shemesh ask “Who can stand in the presence of the LORD, this holy God?”, and how does this chapter treat holiness?
The reapers of Beth-shemesh rejoice to see the ark, but the joy soon turns to mourning: how do you balance joy and reverence before God?
What steps does Samuel ask of the people at Mizpah, and what do the people do in response?
The verb שָׁפַט (shafat, “judge, govern”) defines Samuel's role at the end of the chapter: what kind of leadership does he exercise, and where?
What difference is there between this victory over the Philistines and the defeat of chapter 4, which also began near Ebenezer?
Samuel sets up a stone and says “Thus far the LORD has helped us”: what marker would you set on your path to remember help you received?
What reasons do the elders give for asking for a king, and what model do they want to follow?
The word מִשְׁפָּט (mishpat, “right, custom”) describes “the ways of the king”: what contrast is there with the justice perverted by Samuel's sons in verse 3?
What does the LORD mean by saying the people have rejected Him, and not Samuel?
The people want to be “like all the other nations”: in what areas do you feel the pressure to be like everyone else, and what does it cost?
What route do Saul and his servant take in search of the donkeys, and who has the idea of looking for the man of God?
The text explains that the prophet used to be called a רֹאֶה (ro'eh, “seer”): what does this name suggest about Samuel's role in this story of things lost and found?
While Saul looks for donkeys, God had already spoken to Samuel about him: what does this double perspective show about the way the narrator tells the story?
Saul thinks himself too small for the honor Samuel announces to him: when have you felt this way before an unexpected task?
What three signs does Samuel announce to Saul on the way back, and what does the text say God does with his heart?
The verb נָבָא (nava', “prophesy”) marks Saul's meeting with the prophets: why do the people turn the episode into a proverb?
Saul is chosen by lot before everyone, but he is hiding among the baggage: what does this detail suggest about the new king?
Some follow Saul with their hearts touched, others despise him, and he stays silent: how do you react when people doubt you right at the start of something?
What condition does Nahash impose on the people of Jabesh-gilead, and how much time do they ask for?
The request for a “treaty” uses the verb כָּרַת (karat, literally “cut”): how does the treaty Nahash proposes contrast with what a covenant should guarantee?
What relationship does the chapter establish between the Spirit of God coming upon Saul and the way he mobilizes Israel?
After the victory, Saul refuses to kill those who had despised him: what might this attitude teach about how you deal with those who doubted you?
What questions does Samuel ask the people about his own conduct, and what do the people answer?
Why does Samuel recount Israel's history since Egypt before speaking of the newly chosen king?
The verb יָרֵא (yare', “fear”) appears both in Samuel's warning and in his comfort: what difference is there between the fear of verse 18 and the fear asked for in verse 24?
Samuel says it would be a sin to stop praying for the people: for whom do you feel you have a duty to keep praying or interceding?
What pressures does Saul face at Gilgal while waiting for Samuel, and what does he decide to do on the seventh day?
The word עֹלָה (‘olah, “burnt offering”) appears in Saul's justification: why does offering the burnt offering become the center of the conflict with Samuel?
What does the expression “a man after His own heart” mean in this context, and with whom does it contrast?
What does the lack of blacksmiths in Israel reveal about the people's situation in the face of the Philistines?
Saul says “I felt compelled” to justify a decision made under pressure: in what situations do haste or fear push you to act too soon?
What does Jonathan propose to his armor-bearer, and what sign does he choose to know whether to go up?
How does Saul's oath affect the people during the battle, and why does Jonathan say his father “has brought trouble to the land”?
The דְּבַשׁ (devash, “honey”) Jonathan tastes almost costs him his life: what does this detail reveal about Saul's leadership in this chapter?
Jonathan says nothing can hinder the LORD from saving, “whether by many or by few”: where have you been measuring your possibilities only by the size of your resources?
What do Saul and the people spare from Amalek, and how does Saul describe the mission when he meets Samuel?
The verb נָחַם (nacham, “regret, relent”) appears in verse 11, is denied in 29 and returns in 35: how do you understand this tension in the way the text speaks of God?
What does Samuel mean by “to obey is better than sacrifice,” and why does he compare rebellion to divination?
The command to destroy Amalek is among the hardest in the Bible: what reasons does the text itself give, and how have Jewish and Christian readers dealt with texts like this?
Saul admits he sinned “because I was afraid of the people”: in what situations does the opinion of others weigh more in your decisions than what you know is right?
In what order do Jesse's sons pass before Samuel, and where is David meanwhile?
The chapter speaks of the Spirit of the LORD coming upon David and departing from Saul in the same passage: what does this juxtaposition indicate about the transition between the two?
The word רוּחַ (ruach, “spirit, wind, breath”) appears in opposite senses in this chapter: how does the text distinguish the Spirit that comes upon David from the one that torments Saul?
“Man sees what is visible, but the LORD sees the heart”: what criterion of appearance do you usually use to judge people?
How is Goliath described, what challenge does he issue, and what is the reaction of Saul and Israel?
The verb חָרַף (charaf, “defy, taunt”) passes from Goliath's mouth to David's: how does David change the meaning of the challenge by speaking of “the living God”?
Why does David refuse Saul's armor, and what do the weapons he chooses say about who he is?
According to David, what should the whole earth and “this whole assembly” learn from this battle?
David draws on what he lived while caring for sheep to face something bigger: what past experiences can give you courage for a present challenge?
What gestures does Jonathan make to seal the covenant with David, and what does he give him?
Why does the women's song change the way Saul looks at David?
The verb שָׂכַל (sakal, “act wisely, succeed”) describes David several times: how does this quality relate to Saul's growing fear?
Saul begins to eye David “jealously” after a comparison: how do you deal with it when someone's success seems to diminish your own?
How does Michal help David escape, and what explanation does she give her father?
The verb מָלַט (malat, “escape”) is repeated in David's flight: who helps David escape throughout the chapter, and by what means?
What does it mean that the messengers, and then Saul himself, are seized by the Spirit and prophesy instead of arresting David?
Jonathan defends David before his own father by recalling the good he did: when have you had to speak up for someone at a personal cost?
What sign with the arrows does Jonathan agree on with David, and what was each phrase said to the boy supposed to mean?
Why does Jonathan ask that David's kindness reach his house in the future, and what does this suggest about what he already perceives?
The word שָׁלוֹם (shalom, “peace, well-being”) appears in the plan and in the farewell: what kind of peace is possible between David and Jonathan amid Saul's hostility?
The friendship of David and Jonathan ends this chapter in tears and an oath: what friendships in your life call for loyalty even when it costs dearly?
What does David ask of the priest Ahimelech at Nob, and what does he receive from him?
The bread at Nob is called קֹדֶשׁ (qodesh, “holy”), in contrast to “common” bread: what condition does the priest set for handing it over, and what does this show about the sacred in Israel?
Why does the narrator mention in passing that Doeg the Edomite was there “that day”?
David, afraid, pretends to be insane before Achish: what do you usually do when fear takes over a situation?
Who joins David in the cave of Adullam, and how does the text describe these people?
What tone does Saul use when speaking to his servants, and what do his accusations reveal about his state?
The word כֹּהֵן (kohen, “priest”) is repeated in the massacre at Nob: why do Saul's servants refuse to touch the priests, and who ends up doing it?
David acknowledges “I am responsible” and takes in Abiathar: how do you react when you realize a decision of yours harmed someone else?
Why do David's men hesitate to go to Keilah, and what does David do before deciding?
The verb יָרַד (yarad, “go down”) appears in the command to David and in the question “Will Saul come down?”: how does the chapter use the inquiries of God to guide David's movements?
What does Jonathan do when he “strengthened his hand in God,” and how does this visit differ from the attitude of the Ziphites?
David is saved at the last moment by unexpected news: how do you see the “ways out” that appear when everything seemed closed?
What happens in the cave at En-gedi, what do David's men suggest and what does he actually do?
The word כָּנָף (kanaf, “corner, hem of the robe”) recalls Samuel's torn robe in chapter 15: why does cutting off this corner weigh so heavily on David's conscience?
What leads Saul to weep and say “You are more righteous than I,” and what does he admit he knows about the future?
David says “May the LORD judge between you and me”: in what conflict of yours would you need to hand over vengeance and not act on your own?
How does the text introduce Nabal and Abigail, and how does Nabal respond to the request of David's young men?
What arguments does Abigail use to keep David from taking revenge, and what does she say about his future?
The verb בָרַךְ (barakh, “bless”) appears three times in David's answer: whom does he bless, and what does this show about how he comes to see the encounter?
David thanks the one who kept him from acting “with my own hand”: who has stopped you in a moment of anger, and how did you receive it?
What do David and Abishai find in Saul's camp, and what do they take from it?
The expression “the LORD's anointed,” with מָשִׁיחַ (mashiach, “anointed”), is repeated on David's lips: why does he treat Saul this way even while being pursued by him?
Why does David say that driving him from “the LORD's inheritance” is the same as sending him to serve other gods?
David asks that his life be valued in the LORD's eyes as he valued Saul's: what relationship do you see between the way you treat others and what you hope to receive?
What does David conclude “in his heart,” and where does he go to live with his men and their families?
The verb יָשַׁב (yashav, “live, dwell”) is repeated in David's stay among the Philistines: what does it mean for the future king of Israel to live so long in that land?
How does David deceive Achish about his raids, and what does the narrator seem to think of this strategy by reporting it without comment?
David acts on the thought “one of these days I will be swept away”: how do weariness and fear influence your long-term decisions?
What measures had Saul taken earlier against the mediums, and what leads him to seek one at Endor?
The word אוֹב (’ov, “medium, spirit of the dead”) appears in the prohibition and in Saul's search: what does this contradiction reveal about his situation?
What does Samuel's message to the king take up from earlier chapters, and what does it announce?
After the terrible news, the woman insists on giving Saul food: how can small gestures of care matter in a moment of despair?
Who distrusts David among the Philistines, and what reasons do they give for sending him away?
The verb שׁוּב (shuv, “return”) marks the order to send David back: how does this forced return free him from a dilemma he could not resolve on his own?
How do you read David's answer to Achish, knowing what he had done in chapter 27?
David is excused from something he perhaps should not do: when has someone else's “no” spared you from something worse?
What do David and his men find on arriving at Ziklag, and how do the people react?
The word שָׁלָל (shalal, “plunder, spoil”) is repeated from the Amalekite raid to the sharing: how does the way of sharing the plunder change its meaning?
Why does David decide that those who stayed with the baggage receive an equal share, and why does this become a law in Israel?
What role does the Egyptian servant abandoned by his master play in the turning point of the story?
David “strengthened himself in the LORD his God” when even his own men threatened him: where do you seek strength when those closest to you turn against you?
How do Saul, his sons and his armor-bearer die on Mount Gilboa?
The verb נָפַל (nafal, “fall”) opens and runs through the chapter: what falls does the book of 1 Samuel end by narrating, and how does this contrast with its beginning?
Why do the men of Jabesh-gilead risk their lives for the bodies of Saul and his sons, recalling chapter 11?
The people of Jabesh honor Saul in death out of old gratitude: what kindness received in the past can you still repay?
